<document>
# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
This is the strongest document in the series. It applies the measurement standards the earlier critiques asked for (record-based output, two independent hours measures, randomised comparison, a two-year horizon and a pre-specified mediation test) and engages directly with the competing claims. Most of its conclusions hold up. The most important problem is that the system-log hours measure, as described, doesn't fit the reported numbers, and that affects how the meetings mediation should be read.

## Arithmetic checks

- **Per-hour gains reproduce.** Timesheets: 0.966 / 0.88 = 1.098, or +9.8%. Logs: 0.966 / 0.89 = 1.085, or +8.5%.
- **Mediation shares sum correctly.** 47 + 18 + 35 = 100.
- **Halden continuers reproduce.** 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866, a 13.4% fall in hours, and 96.8 / 0.866 = 1.118, or +11.8%.
- **"About a quarter" is right on the like-for-like measure.** On timesheets the gain fell from 12.5% to 9.8%, a 22% decline.
- **The counter-arm cost figure needs explaining.**
  - 12% more staff at full pay, with output restored to roughly baseline, raises staff cost per contact by about 12%.
  - The reported 9% works if staff are about three-quarters of total cost per contact.
  - The report should state that assumption.
  - Also, 1.12 × 0.83 ≈ 0.93 of baseline staff-hours present, so it's worth showing that 12% more staff actually restores waiting times rather than just throughput.

## 1. The system-log measure doesn't fit as described

The report describes log time as "active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases." Taken literally, that excludes meetings. But meeting time fell sharply in treated offices, so case time should have fallen much less than total hours.

Rough calculation, treated relative to control:

| | Timesheet hours | Meeting hours | Non-meeting hours |
|---|---|---|---|
| Treated, baseline | ~37.9 | 7.4 | ~30.5 |
| Treated, month 24 | ~33.4 (−12%) | 3.9 | ~29.5 |
| Control, baseline → month 24 | ~37.9 (stable) | 7.2 → 7.0 | ~30.7 → ~30.9 |

Relative to control, non-meeting time fell only about 4%.

- **If logs measured case time only,** they should show a fall of about 4%, not 11%. The output per log-measured hour would then be about 0.966 / 0.96 ≈ +0.6%, essentially no gain.
- **A fall of 11% means logs must include meeting time,** for example staff staying logged in during meetings. In that case "active" doesn't mean working on cases, and the log measure is essentially a stricter version of total time worked.

Either way, the report should define exactly what log time captures. The answer determines how to read the mediation result:

- **If the denominator includes meeting time,** cutting meetings raises output per hour largely by definition. Removing hours that produce no cases mechanically raises output per hour. The 47% "explained" share is then partly an accounting identity, not a behavioural mechanism.
- **If the denominator excludes meeting time,** a meetings effect would have to work through something else, such as less fragmentation of case work. But then the 11% figure is unexplained.

The policy reading is the same in both cases: much of the gain comes from cutting time that produced no output. That is real and useful. It is different from people working more productively, and the report should say which it is claiming.

## 2. The mediation test is pre-specified, but not independent

**The hypothesis and the test use the same offices.** The analysis was registered at month 11, before the 24-month data existed, which is a real improvement. But it was generated in these 7 treated offices and tested in the same 7. Meeting reductions persist over time, so the 24-month office-level association overlaps heavily with the month-six correlation (r = 0.71) that prompted the hypothesis. "Confirms" in the summary and "survives a registered test" overstate this. "Is consistent with a pre-specified test in the same trial" is accurate. Independent confirmation needs a different trial.

**There are only 14 clusters.** "A larger sample of office-months" doesn't add independent information, because treatment varies at office level and office-months are not independent. A 95% interval of 28–66% for a mediated share from 14 clusters seems narrow. The report should state the inference method (cluster bootstrap, randomisation inference) and the effective sample size.

**The baseline meeting data are new.** The nine-month report said meeting data were collected only in month six. Here, baseline figures appear (7.4 treated, 7.2 control). Were they reconstructed from historical calendars? If so, say so and note any gaps in coverage. The presence of a baseline is what makes the difference-in-differences on meetings credible.

**The measurement timing should be stated.** Mediators and outcome are both described at 24 months, so the analysis should say over what window each was measured, and confirm that meeting cuts came before output changes.

The no-unmeasured-confounding caveat in the limitations is appropriate. Office-level management quality is the obvious confounder, since better managers may both cut meetings and raise output.

## 3. Contamination of the control group affects the decay estimate

The "unplanned observation" is presented as suggestive evidence about reorganisation. But it is also **contamination of the control arm**, and that changes how the decline should be read.

- In month 15, two of the seven control offices cut meetings and raised output per hour by 4.1%.
- Averaged over seven control offices, that lifts control productivity by roughly 1.2% from month 15 onward.
- That narrows the difference-in-differences gap, so part of the decline from 12.5% to 9.8% may come from the control group improving rather than the treatment effect fading.

The report should:
- show the 24-month estimates excluding the two offices, or adjusting for the audit, as a sensitivity analysis; and
- give an interval for the *change* between nine and 24 months. Both point estimates have overlapping intervals, so the decline itself may not be distinguishable from noise.

The 4.1% figure for the two offices is an uncontrolled before–after comparison and should be described as such. The report already gives most of these caveats.

## 4. The summary mixes measures

The summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months." The 12.5% figure is from timesheets and the 8.5% figure is from logs. The like-for-like decline is 12.5% → 9.8%. The body handles this correctly, but the summary overstates the decline by combining a real change over time with a change of measure.

## 5. The Halden follow-up

**Response.** Fourteen of 23 organisations responded. The nine non-responders are not described, and organisations that reverted or did poorly are plausibly less likely to respond.

**"Upper bound" isn't strictly justified.**
- There is no control group across about 2.5 years since baseline.
- Productivity tools, labour markets and demand all changed over that period, in either direction.
- "Optimistic estimate" is safer than "upper bound."

**Data coverage.** The report should say how many of the 11 continuers had time-tracking data. Earlier, only 17 of the original organisations had both records and time tracking.

**The reversion pattern is reported slightly too neatly.**
- The summary says all three reverters had "client-facing or coverage obligations."
- One was a marketing agency citing client deadlines. That is discretionary work, and it doesn't fit the coverage-bound pattern.
- It's a modest counterexample worth stating plainly rather than absorbing into "client-facing."
- The reverters' output at reversion (88–91) is useful and fits the survivorship argument.

**The Halden paper's own errors aren't addressed.** Section 5 responds to the re-analysis and the meta-analysis, but not to the original working paper. One coauthor is a Halden author. Two points the re-analysis raised are left unresolved:
- the discrepancy over when the nine organisations withdrew, before the schedule started or after it began; and
- the "sector-general" conclusion, which the evidence no longer supports.

A sentence correcting each would make the report more even-handed.

## 6. Smaller points

**Few-cluster inference.** This remains unaddressed, as at nine months. Seven offices per arm need randomisation inference or small-sample corrections.

**Timeliness is still not reported.** The nine-month report raised the risk of backlogs exceeding statutory deadlines. At 24 months that is exactly what should be checked: time to decision and the share of cases near or past the deadline.

**Sick days.** The fall of −27% may still partly reflect fewer scheduled days on which absence can occur, as noted for the earlier papers.

**The response to the re-analysis is fair.**
- Its novelty extrapolation concerned self-reported energy rather than output, so "not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten" engages with a slightly weaker claim than it appears.
- The substantive point still stands: a randomised, record-based, log-measured gain at 24 months is incompatible with "entirely an artifact."
- Two time points cannot rule out continued gradual decay.

**The response to the meta-analysis is correct.** The four long studies being uncontrolled studies using scheduled hours is exactly the confounding I raised when reviewing the meta-analysis. It means the meta-analysis's "no decay" conclusion should be withdrawn.

## Overall

The report's main conclusions are supported:
- The per-hour gain in discretionary public-sector work persists at about 8–10% after two years, somewhat smaller than at nine months.
- Output per employee is slightly below control.
- The coverage-bound arm failed on service and cost.
- Neither "entirely an artifact" nor "no sign of decay" survives.

Before the mechanism claims can be relied on, three things need resolving:
1. **The definition of log time.** It determines whether the meetings mediation is a behavioural mechanism or partly an accounting identity.
2. **The decline's sensitivity to control contamination,** with an interval for the change itself.
3. **"Confirms."** It should be softened to reflect that the hypothesis was tested in the same offices that generated it.

**Across the five documents,** the estimated per-hour gain has narrowed:

| Source | Per-hour gain | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Halden pilot | +23.4% | Uncontrolled, scheduled hours, manager-reported |
| Re-analysis of Halden | +10.8% | Records and actual hours, subset |
| Meta-analysis | +8–10% | Better-designed studies |
| Varden, 24 months | +8.5% | Randomised, log-measured |

**The open questions now are:**
- whether the gain keeps fading;
- how much of it comes from cutting non-productive time, as opposed to people working more productively; and
- whether reorganising work without reducing hours captures most of it. That would need a trial arm that reorganises without cutting hours, which neither study had.

I can draft referee comments on this report, or a short synthesis of the whole series.
